targets.title: On Ends-to-Ends Encryption: Asynchronous Group Messaging with Strong Security Guarantees
targets.authors: Katriel Cohn-Gordon, Cas Cremers, Luke Garratt, Jon Millican, Kevin Milner
targets.venue: ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS)
targets.why_needed: Introduces Asynchronous Ratcheting Trees (ART), the binary-tree key-derivation structure that TreeKEM and BeeKEM both belong to per BeeKEM's own classification. This is the first formal security treatment of tree-structured group key derivation and the definitions of forward secrecy and post-compromise security it uses are the ones the rest of the CGKA line inherits or revises.

targets.title: TreeKEM: Asynchronous Decentralized Key Management for Large Dynamic Groups
targets.authors: Karthikeyan Bhargavan, Richard Barnes, Eric Rescorla
targets.why_needed: The original TreeKEM proposal submitted to the IETF MLS working group: the binary-tree public-key structure where each node's key is derivable from its children, later standardized into RFC 9420. Not indexed on DBLP (a technical report, not a venue paper); verified only against the HAL landing page and the citation string inside BeeKEM's own bibliography.

targets.title: The Messaging Layer Security (MLS) Protocol
targets.authors: Richard Barnes, Benjamin Beurdouche, Raphael Robert, Jon Millican, Emad Omara, Katriel Cohn-Gordon
targets.why_needed: The standardized wire protocol for tree-based continuous group key agreement with a centralized delivery service imposing total order. Every decentralized construction in this domain (DCGKA, BeeKEM, DeCAF) states its contribution as removing this total-order requirement, so the requirement itself must be sourced from the standard that imposes it.

targets.title: The Messaging Layer Security (MLS) Architecture
targets.authors: Benjamin Beurdouche, Eric Rescorla, Emad Omara, Srinivas Inguva, Alan Duric
targets.why_needed: Describes the deployment architecture around RFC 9420: the Delivery Service and Authentication Service roles, how membership changes are proposed and committed, and where the centralization point sits that a decentralized construction must remove or replace.

targets.title: Security Analysis and Improvements for the IETF MLS Standard for Group Messaging
targets.authors: Joël Alwen, Sandro Coretti, Yevgeniy Dodis, Yiannis Tselekounis
targets.why_needed: First formal cryptographic security proof for the MLS/TreeKEM draft, identifying gaps between the informally claimed and formally provable security properties of tree-based CGKA. This is the baseline every later formal-security paper on MLS (Alwen TCC 2020, Klein S&P 2021, Wallez S&P 2025) compares against.

targets.title: Continuous Group Key Agreement with Active Security
targets.authors: Joël Alwen, Sandro Coretti, Daniel Jost, Marta Mularczyk
targets.why_needed: Defines the CGKA security game against an active (not just passive) adversary who can inject malicious messages, the model that BeeKEM's own security proofs (ki-DCGKA game) build on and extend to the decentralized, non-totally-ordered setting.

targets.title: On the Price of Concurrency in Group Ratcheting Protocols
targets.authors: Alexander Bienstock, Yevgeniy Dodis, Paul Rösler
targets.why_needed: Proves lower bounds on the communication and computation cost a group ratcheting protocol must pay to tolerate concurrent updates, the theoretical origin of the O(n)-vs-O(log n) tension that CoCoA, Fork-Resilient CGKA, DeCAF and BeeKEM each attempt to narrow from a different direction.

targets.title: Keep the Dirt: Tainted TreeKEM, Adaptively and Actively Secure Continuous Group Key Agreement
targets.authors: Karen Klein, Guillermo Pascual-Perez, Michael Walter, Chethan Kamath, Margarita Capretto, Miguel Cueto, Ilia Markov, Michelle Yeo, Joël Alwen, Krzysztof Pietrzak
targets.venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (S&P)
targets.why_needed: First CGKA construction with a security proof against an adaptive adversary who chooses which parties to corrupt based on protocol transcripts already seen, closing a gap the CRYPTO 2020 and TCC 2020 proofs left open (they assumed static or non-adaptive corruption).

targets.title: CoCoA: Concurrent Continuous Group Key Agreement
targets.authors: Joël Alwen, Benedikt Auerbach, Miguel Cueto Noval, Karen Klein, Guillermo Pascual-Perez, Krzysztof Pietrzak, Michael Walter
targets.why_needed: A centralized-delivery-service CGKA construction (still requires total order) that tolerates concurrent updates within one epoch at sub-O(n) cost rather than serializing them, the comparison point for BeeKEM's own concurrency handling under partition.

targets.title: On the Worst-Case Inefficiency of CGKA
targets.authors: Alexander Bienstock, Yevgeniy Dodis, Sanjam Garg, Garrison Grogan, Mohammad Hajiabadi, Paul Rösler
targets.why_needed: Proves that no CGKA protocol built black-box from standard public-key encryption can achieve sublinear-in-group-size communication cost in the worst case, holding even in an offline setting where the sequence of group operations is known in advance. This is the specific impossibility result that 'Fair-Weather No More' (2026) narrows and that bears directly on whether BeeKEM's O(log n)-common-case/O(n)-worst-case split, and its retention-parameter tradeoff, are inherent to any decentralized construction or specific to BeeKEM's choice of primitives.

targets.title: A Concrete Treatment of Efficient Continuous Group Key Agreement via Multi-Recipient PKEs
targets.authors: Keitaro Hashimoto, Shuichi Katsumata, Eamonn W. Postlethwaite, Thomas Prest, Bas Westerbaan
targets.venue: ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS)
targets.why_needed: Replaces TreeKEM's pairwise per-node public-key encryptions with a single multi-recipient ciphertext, an alternative cost-reduction mechanism to BeeKEM's tree-and-CRDT approach, still under a centralized delivery service. Gives independent concrete (not just asymptotic) bandwidth figures for the same update operation BeeKEM measures.

targets.title: How to Hide MetaData in MLS-Like Secure Group Messaging: Simple, Modular, and Post-Quantum
targets.authors: Keitaro Hashimoto, Shuichi Katsumata, Thomas Prest
targets.venue: ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS)
targets.why_needed: A generic wrapper that upgrades a non-metadata-hiding CGKA (including TreeKEM and, by the same argument, BeeKEM) into one that hides membership metadata from the delivery infrastructure, and states explicitly that the wrapper composes with post-quantum key-encapsulation. Directly addresses both the metadata-privacy and post-quantum requirements of this domain in one mechanism.

targets.title: Fork-Resilient Continuous Group Key Agreement
targets.authors: Joël Alwen, Marta Mularczyk, Yiannis Tselekounis
targets.why_needed: Defines Fork-Resilience for CGKA under a centralized delivery service that can be made to present different group histories to different members, the same forking threat model BeeKEM's Cross-Fork Security targets for the fully decentralized case with no delivery service at all. The precise formal definition here is what BeeKEM's Cross-Fork Security proof must be checked against for consistency or divergence.

targets.title: TreeSync: Authenticated Group Management for Messaging Layer Security
targets.authors: Théophile Wallez, Jonathan Protzenko, Benjamin Beurdouche, Karthikeyan Bhargavan
targets.why_needed: A machine-checked (F*, DY*) formal specification and proof of the MLS sub-protocol that governs adding, removing, and updating members and keeping every member's view of the group state consistent and authenticated. This is the administered-group-membership half of MLS that a decentralized replacement (BeeKEM's operation-graph replay) must reproduce the guarantees of without a central authority. Distinguished Paper Award at USENIX Security 2023.

targets.title: Cryptographic Administration for Secure Group Messaging
targets.authors: David Balbás, Daniel Collins, Serge Vaudenay
targets.why_needed: Formalizes administrated group messaging, where designated administrators (not every member) can add or remove members and their permissions are themselves cryptographically enforced rather than assumed. Directly on point for the domain's 'administrated and decentralized group membership' axis: states the security definitions and cost of the administrated end of that axis against which any fully peer-symmetric decentralized scheme must be compared.

targets.title: WhatsUpp with Sender Keys? Analysis, Improvements and Security Proofs
targets.authors: David Balbás, Daniel Collins, Phillip Gajland
targets.why_needed: First formal cryptographic model and security proof for Sender Keys, the pairwise-fan-out group-encryption scheme deployed in WhatsApp and Signal, and proposes a modification lowering its total communication cost from quadratic to linear in group size. Also posted to arXiv as 2301.07045. This is the primary source for the Sender Keys O(n^2) cost claim in this domain, which must be cited to this paper rather than stated from memory.

targets.title: Practically-exploitable Cryptographic Vulnerabilities in Matrix
targets.authors: Martin R. Albrecht, Sofía Celi, Benjamin Dowling, Daniel Jones
targets.venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (S&P)
targets.why_needed: Finds and demonstrates exploitable key-confusion and unauthenticated-key-share attacks in the deployed Matrix federated messaging protocol's group-session key-sharing mechanism, a real federated (partially decentralized) group-membership system distinct from the MLS/TreeKEM/DCGKA line. Gives independent evidence of what fails in a real deployed decentralized-adjacent group-key mechanism, as opposed to a paper-only threat model.

targets.title: DeCAF: Decentralizable CGKA with Fast Healing
targets.authors: Joël Alwen, Benedikt Auerbach, Miguel Cueto Noval, Karen Klein, Guillermo Pascual-Perez, Krzysztof Pietrzak
targets.why_needed: A second, independent decentralized CGKA construction from the Alwen/Pietrzak line, explicitly positioned against Weidner et al.'s DCGKA on healing speed after a compromise. This is the direct competing result to both DCGKA and BeeKEM that the domain brief names by mechanism family, and its cost and healing-time figures are the other side's numbers that BeeKEM's comparison table must be checked against.

targets.title: Quarantined-TreeKEM: A Continuous Group Key Agreement for MLS, Secure in Presence of Inactive Users
targets.authors: Céline Chevalier, Guirec Lebrun, Ange Martinelli, Abdul Rahman Taleb
targets.venue: ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS)
targets.why_needed: Modifies TreeKEM to remain secure and continue admitting updates when some members are inactive (offline, not merely slow) for extended periods without excluding them from the group, a direct analogue under a centralized delivery service of the partition-tolerance problem BeeKEM solves in the fully decentralized case. The inactive-member cost figures are a comparison point for BeeKEM's own new-member catch-up cost.

targets.title: Continuous Group-Key Agreement: Concurrent Updates Without Pruning
targets.authors: Benedikt Auerbach, Miguel Cueto Noval, Boran Erol, Krzysztof Pietrzak
targets.why_needed: A propose-and-commit variant of TreeKEM (centralized delivery service) that keeps update cost at Θ(log N) under a moderate rate of concurrent update proposals per commit, without the tree-pruning step earlier schemes needed. Published after BeeKEM's ePrint posting is dated; a direct, recent comparison point for the concurrency-cost figures BeeKEM reports for the decentralized case.

targets.title: TreeKEM: A Modular Machine-Checked Symbolic Security Analysis of Group Key Agreement in Messaging Layer Security
targets.authors: Théophile Wallez, Jonathan Protzenko, Karthikeyan Bhargavan
targets.venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (S&P)
targets.why_needed: A machine-checked symbolic (not just computational) security analysis of the full TreeKEM protocol as standardized, extending the TreeSync formal-methods line to the key-agreement core itself. Published in 2025, after the RFC finalized and after most of the computational-model proofs in this domain, so it is the paper to check for any gap the computational proofs missed.

targets.title: Analyzing Group Chat Encryption in MLS, Session, Signal, and Matrix
targets.authors: Joseph Jaeger, Akshaya Kumar
targets.why_needed: A single unified formal analysis comparing four deployed group-messaging protocols with different membership-administration and delivery-service architectures (MLS's tree-based centralized delivery service, Session's and Signal's Sender-Keys-derived designs, and Matrix's federated design) under one security model. This is the paper to cite for a cross-protocol comparison rather than reasoning from any one protocol's own claims about the others.

targets.title: Tighter Provable Security for TreeKEM
targets.authors: Karen Azari, Andreas Ellison
targets.why_needed: Improves the concrete (not just asymptotic) security bound of the CRYPTO 2020 and TCC 2020 proofs for TreeKEM, which changes the key sizes needed for a given security level. Any concrete-parameter comparison between TreeKEM-family and BeeKEM at matched security levels needs this bound rather than the older, looser ones.

targets.title: Making Post Quantum Key Exchange Efficient: An Implementation with the MLS Protocol
targets.authors: Noah Greene, Britta Hale
targets.why_needed: First benchmarking of hybrid classical/post-quantum ciphersuite combinations inside an actual MLS implementation, measured across group size, CPU cycles, message bytes, and wall-clock runtime, and reports overhead savings against naive post-quantum-only ciphersuites. This supplies measured post-quantum cost figures for the tree-based line that BeeKEM^PQ (sketched, not benchmarked, in the BeeKEM paper) can be checked against.

targets.title: Generic Anonymity Wrapper for Messaging Protocols
targets.authors: Lea Thiemt, Paul Rösler, Alexander Bienstock, Rolfe Schmidt, Yevgeniy Dodis
targets.venue: ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS)
targets.why_needed: Formalizes an Authenticated Anonymity Wrapper that hides sender/recipient metadata for both two-party and group messaging protocols with forward anonymity and post-compromise anonymity, states it gives stronger anonymity guarantees than Sender Keys achieves natively, and the paper states Signal is evaluating deployment. Signal's own evaluation is a claim to attribute to Signal if repeated, not to be stated as fact from this paper alone. A second, independent metadata-hiding mechanism for group messaging beyond the CCS 2022 wrapper, letting the two be compared on cost and threat model.

targets.title: Bots can Snoop: Uncovering and Mitigating Privacy Risks of Bots in Group Chats
targets.authors: Kai-Hsiang Chou, Yi-Min Lin, Yi-An Wang, Jonathan Weiping Li, Tiffany Hyun-Jin Kim, Hsu-Chun Hsiao
targets.why_needed: Measures the privacy exposure created when a third-party bot is added as a full group member in existing group-messaging deployments (it receives every message any tree-based or Sender-Keys scheme delivers to a member) and proposes SnoopGuard, a tree-based CGKA extended with selective Internal Group Anonymity so a member's identity can be hidden from specific other members, including bots, without excluding them from the group. Bears on any design that treats 'group member' as a single undifferentiated access class.

targets.title: Decentralized Continuous Group Key Agreement for UAV Ad-Hoc Network
targets.authors: Hong, Zhou, Yang, Shen, Zheng (full given names not resolved from Crossref metadata)
targets.venue: Machine Learning for Cyber Security (ML4CS), Lecture Notes in Computer Science
targets.why_needed: Applies decentralized CGKA specifically to an unmanned-aerial-vehicle ad-hoc network, a deployment setting where network partition from mobility and range is the normal operating condition rather than an edge case. Directly relevant to whether BeeKEM's conjectured retention-parameter tradeoff between cross-branch recovery and forward secrecy holds up against measurements from a real partition-prone physical network, as opposed to a simulated one.

targets.title: Amigo: Secure Group Mesh Messaging in Realistic Protest Settings
targets.authors: David Inyangson, Sarah Radway, Tushar M. Jois, Nelly Fazio, James Mickens
targets.venue: ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS)
targets.why_needed: A group-messaging design for Bluetooth-range mesh networks (no internet, no central server, frequent partition) evaluated under a protest threat model, the most physically decentralized deployment setting in this domain. Its group-key mechanism and measured costs under partition and device churn are the comparison point for whether BeeKEM-style designs, built for internet-connected causal broadcast, extend to a fully offline mesh.

targets.title: Auditable Continuous Group Key Agreement
targets.authors: Easwar Vivek Mangipudi, Maddie Gorman, Sasha Levinshteyn
targets.why_needed: Posted after BeeKEM. Adds an auditability extension to CGKA with a Rust prototype and a post-quantum custom multi-stage STARK proof system, targeting adaptive post-quantum security in the secure-erasure model. Directly answers the domain brief's instruction to seek anything published after BeeKEM, and is a second post-quantum decentralized-adjacent CGKA construction to compare against BeeKEM^PQ.

targets.title: Fair-Weather No More: Guaranteed Efficiency in Secure Group Messaging
targets.authors: James Bartusek, Nir Bitansky, Yevgeniy Dodis, Rachit Garg, David J. Wu
targets.why_needed: Posted after BeeKEM. Presents the first CGKA protocol with provably logarithmic WORST-CASE (not just common-case) complexity, based on a falsifiable post-quantum assumption (decomposed LWE), achieving post-compromise security but not forward secrecy in the base construction, and forward secrecy only at the cost of a linear-time refresh in a random-oracle extension. Its abstract states this narrows, but does not close, the gap the CRYPTO/TCC 2022 impossibility results (Bienstock et al.) opened. This is the single most direct available answer to the domain brief's question of whether BeeKEM's retention-parameter tradeoff is inherent: it shows worst-case-sublinear CGKA is possible in principle but that forward secrecy still forces a linear-cost operation somewhere, from a completely different (complexity-theoretic, not partition-tolerance) angle than BeeKEM's own conjecture.

targets.title: Benchmarking of the Amortized Post Quantum Combiner for MLS
targets.authors: Britta Hale, Tian, Wang (given names not resolved from Crossref metadata)
targets.venue: Security Standardisation Research (SSR), Lecture Notes in Computer Science
targets.why_needed: Measures the amortized cost of a hybrid classical/post-quantum key combiner integrated into MLS across repeated group operations, rather than a single-operation snapshot. A second, independent post-quantum-MLS cost measurement (after Greene and Hale 2025) from an overlapping author, useful for checking whether the 2025 single-run figures hold up amortized over a session.

targets.title: A Formal Security Analysis of the Signal Messaging Protocol
targets.authors: Katriel Cohn-Gordon, Cas Cremers, Benjamin Dowling, Luke Garratt, Douglas Stebila
targets.venue: IEEE European Symposium on Security and Privacy (EuroS&P); extended version Journal of Cryptology 2020
targets.why_needed: The formal security proof of the Double Ratchet as used in two-party Signal sessions, defining the forward-secrecy and post-compromise-security properties in the specific asynchronous, out-of-order-delivery setting that group protocols must also handle. Sender Keys and every pairwise-fan-out group scheme (WhatsApp, early Signal groups) is built from pairwise Double Ratchet sessions between this protocol's endpoints, so its guarantees and failure modes are inherited claims, not independent ones, for the group case.

targets.title: On Post-Compromise Security
targets.authors: Katriel Cohn-Gordon, Cas Cremers, Luke Garratt
targets.why_needed: Coins and formally defines Post-Compromise Security: the guarantee that a party recovers security after a key compromise once it takes further protocol steps, without needing to detect the compromise first. Every later paper in this domain that claims 'post-compromise security' (DCGKA, BeeKEM included) is claiming this specific, cited definition, not an informal synonym for 'heals eventually.'

targets.title: SoK: Secure Messaging
targets.authors: Nik Unger, Sergej Dechand, Joseph Bonneau, Sascha Fahl, Henning Perl, Ian Goldberg, Matthew Smith
targets.venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (S&P)
targets.why_needed: Systematization of Knowledge covering the secure-messaging landscape as of 2015, including the trust-establishment, conversation-security, and transport-privacy properties every later group-messaging paper in this domain positions itself against. Predates MLS and the CGKA line, so it establishes the pre-existing terminology and evaluation criteria (rather than criteria invented by any single later paper) that a Pareto-style comparison in this project should reuse or explicitly justify departing from.

targets.title: Rollercoaster: An Efficient Group-Multicast Scheme for Mix Networks
targets.authors: Daniel Hugenroth, Martin Kleppmann, Alastair R. Beresford
targets.why_needed: From the same author group as DCGKA (Weidner, Kleppmann, Hugenroth, Beresford), this paper covers the metadata-privacy half the domain brief asks for: an efficient scheme for delivering group-multicast ciphertexts through a mix network so the network operator cannot learn group membership or message timing correlations from delivery traffic, complementary to (not a replacement for) the key-agreement mechanism itself.

targets.title: Mesh Messaging in Large-Scale Protests: Breaking Bridgefy
targets.authors: Martin R. Albrecht, Jorge Blasco, Rikke Bjerg Jensen, Lenka Mareková
targets.why_needed: Demonstrates concrete message-forgery, denial-of-service, and user-deanonymization attacks against Bridgefy, a deployed Bluetooth-mesh messaging application used during real protests, caused by its complete absence of end-to-end encryption or authenticated group key agreement in its group/broadcast messages at the time of the study. Establishes, as a measured fact from a real deployment rather than a hypothetical, what specifically fails when a mesh-network messaging app ships without the cryptographic mechanisms the rest of this domain provides.

targets.title: Non-Interactive Key Exchange
targets.authors: Eduarda S. V. Freire, Dennis Hofheinz, Eike Kiltz, Kenneth G. Paterson
targets.why_needed: Formally defines Non-Interactive Key Exchange (NIKE): a scheme where two parties compute a shared key from each other's static public key alone, with no protocol messages exchanged. BeeKEM's core mechanism (each inner tree node's secret is derived by NIKE between its two children) is built directly on this primitive and its security definition; the strength of BeeKEM's proofs is bounded by the strength of the NIKE security notion this paper supplies.

targets.title: Making CRDTs Byzantine Fault Tolerant
targets.authors: Martin Kleppmann
targets.venue: Workshop on Principles and Practice of Consistency for Distributed Data (PaPoC), co-located with EuroSys
targets.why_needed: BeeKEM's paper states directly that BeeKEM is itself a CRDT (a data structure whose merge operation converges regardless of the arrival order of concurrent updates) and that it requires only causal broadcast, not any stronger delivery guarantee. This paper is the source for what 'Byzantine fault tolerant' means for a CRDT specifically (tolerating participants who send different, contradictory operations to different recipients) and what a causal-broadcast layer underneath a CRDT must additionally guarantee for that tolerance to hold; it is a precondition this domain's selection places on the transport and dissemination layer, not on the key-agreement layer itself.

targets.title: Byzantine Eventual Consistency and the Fundamental Limits of Peer-to-Peer Databases
targets.authors: Martin Kleppmann, Heidi Howard
targets.why_needed: Proves a lower bound: no peer-to-peer database (or, by the same argument, a decentralized CGKA state machine) can simultaneously guarantee Byzantine fault tolerance, eventual consistency, and availability under network partition without an additional trust assumption between at least some pairs of participants. Bears directly on whether BeeKEM's conjectured tradeoff between cross-branch recovery and forward secrecy under partition is a consequence of BeeKEM's specific design choices or an instance of this more general impossibility result for any leaderless, partition-tolerant replicated system.
